H_hierarchical.evidence: The controller is organized into Normal, Rank1, Rank2, and Rank3 modes; privileged modes reuse collective-operation dispatch internally for same-rank calls, but the paper does not define a deep named substate tree.

G_guards_arith.evidence: Normal-mode output is derived from a Karnaugh expression over movement state, call direction, cabin/floor call, and closest-call variables; privileged modes add rank, before/after, and en-route conditions.

A_actions_nontrivial.evidence: Transitions perform call cancellation, memory storage/reset, nearest-floor stop, passenger announcement, direct dispatch to the privileged caller, and mode return after fulfillment.

F_fault_recovery.evidence: Rank1 acts as a cross-cutting escape path from Rank2, Rank3, or Normal: the elevator stops, evacuates passengers, cancels lower-priority traffic, and serves Rank1 directly.

T1_cross_section_element.evidence: Mode summaries are in the Introduction, guard logic and Karnaugh conditions are in section 2.2.1, and per-rank transition actions are spread across sections 2.2.2.1-2.2.2.3 and Table 2.

T2_implicit_domain_term.evidence: Terms such as collective operation, en-route closeness, most appropriate call, and privileged use require mapping elevator-dispatch domain notions into state-transition guards.

T3_implicit_action_from_prose.evidence: Most actions are stated under the relevant Rank1, Rank2, Rank3, or Normal-mode paragraphs, so state-action attribution is largely local despite being prose.

T4_multivar_arith_guard.evidence: The Karnaugh-derived normal-mode condition combines multiple boolean variables for elevator movement, halt/stop status, call direction, cabin calls, and proximity.

T5_composite_internal_behavior.evidence: Privileged rank modes have their own override/entry behavior while also embedding collective-operation behavior for same-rank calls.

T6_global_cross_cutting_recovery.evidence: A Rank1 request preempts Rank2, Rank3, and Normal through the same stop-evacuate-direct-service rule.

C1_speculative_dfs.evidence: The paper does not define explicit initial pseudo-state chains or non-trivial composite initialization.

C2_expr_ir_smt.evidence: The Karnaugh and priority guards combine many boolean conditions, making expression normalization and consistency checking useful.

C3_forced_and_aspect.evidence: Rank1 preemption applies across three high-level modes, so a forced transition can encode one cross-cutting rule instead of duplicating it.

C4_abstract_action.evidence: Announcement, call cancellation, and call-memory updates are abstract control effects, although much of the elevator movement behavior is concrete.

key_nl_quotes: When in either Rank2, Rank3 or Normal mode
Collective operation answers same direction calls according to proximity
one_line_pitch: A rank-priority elevator supervisor with Karnaugh-style multi-variable guards, mode-local collective dispatch, and global Rank1 preemption directly stresses guard, action, and hierarchy weaknesses in Umple-style baselines.
rationale: This is a strong stress-test because the paper gives real control logic rather than a toy FSM: rank modes, same-rank collective dispatch, multi-variable guard synthesis, and non-trivial transition effects are all present. The hardest baseline trap is the cross-cutting Rank1 preemption rule, which must be propagated from multiple modes while preserving cancellation, announcement, and direct-dispatch actions. It has no hard-exclusion features and has enough paper evidence to construct a meaningful reference state machine.
